text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

AMP Society is linking with Nikko Securities to sell Japanese retail investors up to A$200 million worth of units in the AMP-Nikko Dynamic Australia Fund. AMP Investment Management managing director Andrew Threadgold said the move could see AMP wanting to become a trust bank in the longer term, servicing the pension fund industry in Japan. Page 1.

Gold assays recorded from rock chips at Helix Resources' Tunkillia site have sparked a new gold rush in South Australia's Gawler Craton and boosted Helix's market capitalisation from A$18 million in mid-November to A$141 million at Friday's closing price of A$3.35. J.B. Were & Son is also enthusiastic about the find, backing Helix for the past months and set to act as broker to a share issue that will raise another A$27 million for exploration. Page 1.

About 1,100 delegates from the Asia-Pacific region will attend the fourth National Trade and Investment Outlook Conference in Melbourne today, with Trade Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer chairing tomorrow's opening plenary session of the conference, which generated at least A$158 million of new export business and investment in 1995. Page 4.

Outlining News Ltd's strategy yesterday, executive chairman Ken Cowley said News had given up on the idea of controlling John Fairfax Holdings Ltd and he hoped Canadian publisher Conrad Black, who holds a 25 percent stake, would obtain clear control. Cowley also said News wanted to expand in television by owning more of the Seven Network Ltd. Page 21.

As managing director of RG Capital, Tim Hughes is charged with the job of ensuring game show king Reg Grundy's personal fortune of about A$500 million returns better than bank interest. The most visible moves RG Capital has made so far have been the unsuccessful takeover bid for Sunshine Broadcasting and the successful bid for radio network Sea-FM. Page 21.

North Ltd has reported a first-quarter, after-tax profit of A$15.3 million, down from A$20 million and has conceded that some of its key businesses are operating at reduced profit levels. It said the rising value of the Australian dollar could affect earnings over the longer term. Page 23.
THE AUSTRALIAN

News Ltd executive chairman Ken Cowley yesterday predicted Ansett Australia was set to return to profit, with rising turnover and cost savings introduced by the group's new executive team expected to lift the bottom line. Ansett's local operations suffered an A$18.6 million operating loss in 1995/96. Page 17.

AME Mineral Economics coal analyst Clyde Henderson says the Export Coal 1997 study warns that a soaring dollar and predicted lower prices for steaming and semi-coking coal threaten the profitability of Australian coal miners. he study comes as producers battle with their Japanese customers to win higher prices for coking and steaming coal. Page 17.

The United States-based Commodity Futures Trading Commission is expected to give the Sydney Futures Exchange the green light to market its New Zealand investments to U.S. investors during international Futures Week '96 which begins today in Sydney. The move recognises the SFE's standing in the Asia-Pacific region. Page 17.

Italian food and dairy giant Parmalat SpA, under its Australian wing Parmalat Australia, is building an export base in Australia, using fresh local produce to secure lucrative South-East Asian markets. The company derives 60 percent of its sales outside Italy. Page 17.

Argyle Diamond Mines managing director Gordon Gilchrist said yesterday a decision over the extension of the life of the Argyle diamond mine has been put off until at least the middle of next year. Gilchrist said a technical evaluation on taking the mine underground would not be considered by the board before March. Page 19.

Ericsson AB senior executive Johan Siberg, the president of Ericsson's telephones and terminals consumer products division, says peoples' appetite for mobile phones will continue as less traditional users begin to take up the technology. Siberg says mobile phones may eventually reach 100 percent penetration in Australia. Page 19.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

There are growing expectations that the National Australia Bank will launch an all-out raid on the Advance Bank in an attempt to build a blocking stake to stall its merger with St George Bank. Further movement in the banking sector is expected as rumours circulate that Westpac may launch a A$1.3 billion bid for the Bank of Melbourne this week. Page 33.

Changes in the housing industry, such as low inflation, lower immigration levels and a lesser cultural need for Australians to own their own home, has seen the industry predict that a recovery from its current slump will never match the peak in 1994. Page 33.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics will on Wednesday release its estimates of growth in gross domestic product for the September quarter. The figures are expected to show a deceleration in annual growth and could put the federal government's economic management on the line. Page 33.

Forecaster BIS Shrapnel predicts the New South Wales construction industry will attain its fourth consecutive year of growth, with an extra A$570 million worth of projects, sparked mainly by the fever of the 2000 Olympics, to commence in the state this financial year. Page 33.

The New South Wales Supreme Court will hear a case on Tuesday that involves the Commonwealth Bank applying for a court order restraining one of its former litigants from distributing copies of a speech made in New South Wales Parliament about the Bank and a former CBA loans manager two weeks ago. Page 35.

While not an official inquiry, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission is reviewing pricing contracts between growers and processors across all areas of the rural community in the lead-up to de-regulation. The ACCC is looking for anti-competitive pricing arrangements and is forcing changes where needed. Page 35.
THE AGE

As the Reserve Bank holds its final meeting for 1996 tomorrow, few economists are expecting a further cut in interest rates following cautious comments by Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane last week. Twenty-nine economists surveyed by Reuters gave the opinion that there was now only a one-in-10 chance of another rate cut this year. Page C1.

BHP's land holdings in the Newcastle area, in New South Wales' Hunter Valley, are immense, and include huge tracts in the centre of the city, kilometres of absolute beachfront in the southern suburbs, and broad acres in the western suburbs. With these holdings, BHP is now taking on the role of property developer in an attempt to create a new industrial heart for Newcastle to replace the steelworks it has operated there for over 80 years. Page C1.

South Australian Treasurer Stephen Baker yesterday confirmed that a 30-storey office complex at 333 Collins Street in Melbourne, owned by the South Australian Government, has been sold to an unnamed group for A$243 million. The sale sees South Australia lose almost half a billion dollars on the deal. Page C1.

The National Trade and Investment Outlook Conference opens in Melbourne tonight with 1,200 Australian and international business leaders and officials attending. The conference has attracted some of the big names in Asian business and will also hear treasurers from three countries. Page C2.

Melbourne-based medical research investment company Rancoo Ltd is currently financing research to develop a cure for HIV and cancer. The research looks at using gene technology to stimulate the human immune system. Rancoo is pinning its hopes on the success of the research by its 43 percent-owned Virax Pty Ltd. Page C2.

According to the prospects and trends survey taken over the past 12 months by the Victorian Employers' Chamber of Commerce and Industry, a net balance of 50 percent of small manufacturing firms reported a fall in profit in the September quarter, and across all industries, businesses with fewer than 100 employees suffered the most. Page C2.
